content: Cellular respiration is the process organisms use to convert food energy into ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the cell's immediate energy currency. The complete process occurs in three main stages: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle), and oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport chain). Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, breaking glucose (a 6-carbon molecule) into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules while producing a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters mitochondria and is converted to acetyl-CoA, releasing carbon dioxide. The citric acid cycle then metabolizes acetyl-CoA, generating 2 ATP, 6 NADH, and 2 FADHâ per glucose molecule. These electron carriers (NADH and FADHâ) deliver high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons move down the chain, their energy pumps hydrogen ions across the membrane, creating a concentration gradient. ATP synthase uses this gradient's potential energy to synthesize ATP from ADP and phosphateâa process called chemiosmosis. Altogether, aerobic respiration produces about 30-32 ATP molecules per glucose. During intense exercise, when oxygen demand exceeds supply, muscles rely on anaerobic respiration (glycolysis followed by fermentation), which produces only 2 ATP per glucose and generates lactic acid as a byproduct, contributing to muscle fatigue.

scenario.title: Cellular Power Race
scenario.content: Students manage virtual cyclists in a race, balancing energy production with physiological constraints. The simulation visualizes cellular processes within muscle cells, showing glucose breakdown, electron transport, and ATP synthesis in real-time. Students make strategic decisions about food intake (carbohydrates, fats, proteins) and exercise intensity, observing how these choices affect metabolic pathways and energy availability. The simulation demonstrates the transition between aerobic and anaerobic respiration as oxygen availability changes, highlighting the trade-offs between efficiency and power output. Visual indicators show oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, and lactic acid accumulation. Interactive elements allow students to zoom between organismal, cellular, and molecular perspectives to connect macroscopic performance with microscopic processes. Challenge scenarios teach energy management for different race conditions, from sprints to endurance events.

hypothesis.description: Students will trace energy transformations in cellular respiration by following carbon compounds through metabolic pathways. They will compare aerobic and anaerobic processes in terms of efficiency and output, and explain how cellular energy production adapts to different physiological demands and nutrient availability.
